newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's 1997 budget focuses on helping poor.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's 1997 budget focuses on helping poor.

text.p: Jordan's Finance Minister Marwan Awad said on Monday the country's 1997 state spending of 1.92 billion dinars ($2.7 billion) would help the poor as it steps up IMF-directed market reforms.

"What has been allocated additionally and exceptionally is the high rise in the social safety net, including a programme that is being prepared, that will definitely reflect on income levels and prosperity of citizens," Awad said.

Awad, who was announcing projected state spending in 1997 -- representing an 11 percent rise from 1996 adjusted budget figures -- said this left a deficit without foreign aid of 3.9 percent of GDP, or 225 million dinars.
The budget deficit is expected to be a readjusted 237 million dinars in 1996, or 4.6 percent of GDP.

Officials say expanding projects to help Jordan's poor has topped Jordan's economic agenda after riots broke out last August in the underdeveloped south of the country, mainly blamed on widespread poverty and erosion of living standards.

Officials say they are now discussing with the World Bank a $200-$300 million social package to which other donors will contribute, timed for the last two years of IMF reforms. The new budget includes for the first time a seven million dinar allocation for a social safety net.
Economists and officials alike express growing fears of the potential of social unrest with a widening gap between poor and rich that could derail new IMF reforms begun in 1996.
World Bank estimates put poverty among Jordan's 4.2 million people at about 20 percent with a 15 percent unemployment rate.
Awad said expected real GDP growth was estimated at 5.2 percent in 1996 -- lower than a widely estimated six percent -- with a target of 6.5 percent set in 1997.

Jordan is seen by economists as having faired well under an IMF reform package since an economic crisis in 1989 totally wiped out foreign reserves. It has since achieved fiscal and monetary stability, helping cut its budget deficit to less than five percent from a high of 24 percent of GDP in 1990.

Awad said current expenditure was forecast to rise 8.2 percent in 1997 to 1.481 billion dinars. It includes 72 million dinars allocated for fixed cash payments to compensate for steep bread price hikes last August after record grain prices.
Awad said even if local bread prices followed the fall in world wheat prices, the government would still offer these cash payments to citizens.
A 22 percent rise in capital expenditure in 1997 to 435 million dinars was to boost investment and growth, Awad said.
Total state revenues, including foreign aid of 169 million dinars, were forecast to reach 1.860 billion dinars, an increase of six percent from 1996 readjusted budget figure, Awad said.
The draft budget, approved after some alterations by the cabinet on Saturday, reflects accelerated IMF agreed reforms in 1997-1998. It will be sent to parliament soon for approval.
Awad said he was optimistic that Jordan would be able to reduce its budget deficit by the end of a final third year of expanded IMF-directed reforms in 1998 to 2.5 percent of GDP.

Awad said the 1997 draft budget did not include any new measures for tax hikes but stressed that a projected 8.2 percent rise in local revenue to 1.691 billion dinars in 1997 from the previous year would be attained by enhanced tax collection.
